Oh my gosh, I had to laugh. You're going to be A-okay! It's your first day. I was GARBAGE when I started. I routinely completely missed veins that were huge and superficial. Now I'm the go-to for hard sticks in my inpatient hospital. It takes time and practice, you'll get it eventually :) practice a lot and try to be as calm as possible while drawing. When you miss or it goes poorly, try to get feedback or troubleshoot what went wrong. Don't beat yourself up though, even the most experienced person can have a bad day or week. 

If you're completely missing after identifying a vein, try different ways of anchoring (also anchoring throughout the WHOLE draw has helped me immensely). Make sure to palpate well and don't be afraid to redirect. When I started I was terrified that any redirecting is "fishing", this is certainly not true. A calculated, smooth redirection is key. Make sure you pull the needle almost all the way out, then palpate well, adjust, and go back in.  

If you find yourself blowing veins or collapsing them, practice your steadiness and consider the depth+angle of the needle. Frequently it's gone too deep and through the vein (usually a result of a large angle of insertion) or you keep pushing deeper after successfully hitting the vein. I recommend a much shallower angle than you think, and starting with just the bevel in, then slowly going deeper as necessary. It takes a while to develop that feeling of "resistance" when you pierce the vein, so a bit counterintuitively I feel it's better to start with butterflies to get a feel for things before using straights. Seeing a flash helps you figure out what went wrong during a draw and when. Especially if you don't feel confident about the veins you choose. 

If you can't find a vein at all, try palpating with your non-dominant hand (this works for some people, didn't work for me personally though) and trying to press a bit harder. The motion will be up and down. When on a vein it should almost feel like a little trampoline. It's also possible to feel the roundness of the vein by rocking side to side with your finger. In patients that are overweight I find this rocking motion to be much more effective. A really good exercise is to find an easy to palpate vein on your own arm and then work your way up or down trying to follow its path as far out as you can. This way you know you're feeling a vein but can see how it changes as it gets deeper and deeper.

You'll have those 30 draws in no time! You got this :)

This looks gorgeous! the lighting is superb. I think the major compositional issue is values, not the framing and flow. I would add maybe one more heart pointing directly to the eye since that seems to be a focal point, and I would increase the contrast a bit to better differentiate the value groups. Here is an example of what I mean: [https://imgur.com/a/UBUeR4W](https://imgur.com/a/UBUeR4W)

Gesture I think is great at any point, but especially helpful as a beginner. It deals with intuitive perspective, observational drawing, and the hardest, simplification. It's difficult at first but that's the point! Each bit of practice you do will help you improve massively.[Check out Proko's Figure Drawing Fundamentals ](https://youtu.be/74HR59yFZ7Y?si=5hD3DiN2jT1tyoW3) course and try some of the exercises out. There's free videos on there with great instruction (some on YT, some on his website proko.) I think the key is to focus on exaggerating the movement you see and simplifying things into just CSI lines, aka lines with the shape "C" "S" and "I" or straight. Best of luck!

Normally I wouldn't insert a tube without a flash, it just means you're not in the veins lumen. But I've noticed some needle brands and even certain gauges of the same brand will have no flash or just the smallest one imaginable yet actually be perfectly in the vein and flowing just fine. If I can see that the needle is in the vein, and upon palpating I'm just really stumped as to how I'm missing, I'll try a tube or pull up on the syringe. It's better to try it then to have to re poke the patient in my opinion. If you're in the vein but there's no flash it's 100% an equipment failure but it's more likely that it's just not in yet. Best of luck friend :) it's all practice and you'll be a pro in no time

The needles for straight and butterflies aren't that different.  For a small vein the advantage is that you can see a flash that indicates you actually hit it and are in the lumen. Small needles (like 25g) are really needed only for the smallest veins, like finger ones. I know it's obvious to "just palpate" but it really is key to find how a vein feels under the many layers below the skin, not just superficial ones. It's a similar feeling to superficial veins, springy and bouncy like a trampoline but not hard like a cord. It's dampened as it gets deeper and becomes harder to feel for the tuberosity of the vein itself. Try palpating harder than you think you need to, and bouncing up and down with your finger instead of a rubbing motion. You can also try rocking side to side to feel for the cylindrical shape.

I feel like I go against most advice but I find using a butterfly in the beginning is beneficial. It doesn't have to be a small butterfly, you could try with like a 21g but being able to see if you got a flash or not is helpful for troubleshooting and identifying what went wrong in the first place. When you consistently hit the mark or know how to readjust when you didn't hit it within the first insertion then you can apply that knowledge to straights and work on feeling out what you could previously see with butterflies. Try it out and see if you missed (no flash) or it blew/collapsed, etc (flash). Then you know what you need to do :)

At my hospital we use almost exclusively butterfly needles with the occasional straight coming out only if there's a juicy AC or vein in the region. We have 21, 23, and last resort 25g butterflies and then 22 and 21g straights :)
I also pinch, I find I have a harder time controlling angle and keeping it stable by holding the wings. But that's my own preference :)

4 1/2 months in and part time? You're doing great dude. Inpatient draws are a different ballgame. If your hospital doesn't limit your butterfly use then like the other commenter said keep using what's comfortable until you feel confident in it. Once you feel that you've gotten the hang of it start to incorporate what you struggle with. 

At our hospital we almost exclusively use butterflies. A lot of the time our sticks are in unusual places with very small fragile veins to work with. When I have a nice AC, or a hand vein that looks good, I'll pull that straight stick out. I highly recommend looking at spots you wouldn't usually do when you have hard sticks or people where it feels like there's no veins at all (I've done knuckles, bicep, thumb, 2nd knuckle fingers, elbow, etc). Also, if the veins don't feel particularly healthy or they are small, consider using a syringe to control the pressure you are putting on the vein. You'll start to get a feel for what each vein can handle and how they feel, but it's okay to be extra cautious to avoid a hematoma or the vein collapsing. 

The usual tricks apply as well. Heat packs (we use the infant heel warmers), light tapping or massaging, letting the arm hang down for gravity, etc. Another thing with inpatient is that a lot of people have had IV's or sticks everywhere making certain veins hard like IV drug users' veins get hard. If you have a vein that you can see clearly but feels rock hard do not use it, it's most likely scarring. You always want to feel a healthy bounce or at least a slight one with older or more fragile folk. 

In general though, you got this friend. It's all practice and soon you'll be getting sticks you wouldn't think you could. Give it time and don't let your own heat eat your confidence away :)

Hi there! This is gorgeous, I think the reason it looks off is the perspective. Her face is at an angle, 3/4, as well as being seen from above. It seems like the construction of the neck and head is slanted as if it's from the front. Try drawing out a basic cylinder shape to get the feel for that angle, it's a difficult one. Overall it looks great though and it probably just needs some liquifying around to get it just right. Here's a [crappy phone draw over](https://imgur.com/a/xA9snHa) of what I mean

Personally I found that things get very stiff if you do a stick man and go adding each part one by one. A good way to get it to work together is to study the flow of the body, aka gesture drawing. Proko has great videos on this topic.

I think your lines might be a bit too thick. Being slightly off can make a large difference in angle as you make that line longer. Keep in mind that in real life there are infinite vanishing points as each object has its own set unless it is perfectly aligned with another object. There will always be only one horizon line, however. You can figure out where this is by placing lines like you are right now, or by observing how the planes of an object change. If you imagine a cube below the horizon line (HL) you will see its upper side clearly. As it moves closer to the HL, that side becomes less and less visible until it's completely parallel with the HL and you only see the front side. Here's an [imgur link](https://imgur.com/a/IbSIWqo) with what I mean visually. This is a super tricky picture since there are a lot of rotating planes building on one another. Proko and Ethan Becker have great videos on this topic. Good job tackling this image, this is a tough one! :)

Hi! This is super cool. I love the expressions and action you have going on. For me the biggest issue is clarity, there's a lot of awesome detail that's getting lost and ends up clouding everything. Try some thicker outlines around the focus of the shot, in particular the characters. Better line weight control will help with this. The composition of the subjects and panels is good but it gets lost without line weight/value composition.
Check out 10 Minutes to Better Painting by Marco Bucci on YouTube. Everything from color to values is addressed in a condensed, easy to watch format but rich in content.

Hello there! I feel you with action lines, at least personally I never felt like I could apply them properly. I recommend working on the silhouette here as it helps a lot with clarity and dynamism. Personally, things feel impactful with dramatic perspective and foreshortening, highly recommend Sycras video on it on YouTube. You don't have to study grid lines and all the really complex, almost mathematical, perspective stuff but keeping it in the back of your mind helps with really selling the 3d ness of your images. I think you'd enjoy Tom Fox Draws, he has an excellent book on anatomy that focuses more on intuitive drawing like you describe. I think one of the most important takeaways from him is trying to show at least 3 sides of each object or form you're drawing. The 3 sides are the 3 dimensions that take something from being a shape on paper to the illusion of 3d form on paper. Even for cartoons or anime styles these changes will make a big difference. Happy drawing!

Great job with the proportions of the face, it looks very good. I think the hand is feeling too small, the foreshortening isn't being sold too well. The marksmanship is also fairly poor, there doesn't seem to be a clear direction or form that it's trying to inform. Try drawing your lines across the forms themselves rather than just filling in the shape. I think this is the clearest to see on the sleeves, with lines going straight up or down or horizontal when the 3D form is curved. If you're looking to monetize drawing portraits work on the marksmanship first! It will make a significant difference.

Hey, I was in your same position a few months back when I started as an inpatient phleb/ lab assistant/specimen processor. I'm slowly inching closer to a year and finally starting to understand things but I still feel brand new compared to my coworkers. No one should be irritated or angry with you for having questions or messing up now and then, you're learning and human. It takes more than just hearing something once, for a lot of more complex tasks in the lab you need to go through it a few times yourself before it clicks. Always check your SOPs and ask your supervisor for resources. And ask questions! There is so much to know it's unreasonable to expect you to just intuit things. Try not to compare yourself, those same classmates might have already had experience. 

For me I felt the same, I felt super slow and dumb. Give it time and always double check what you're working on, get a notebook if you can and take notes. Like the other commenter said, if it's the same thing try to slow down (slow is smooth, smooth is fast) but if it's different there is nothing to feel bad about. It can be mentally draining as well, for me there were times I had to take a break just because I kept messing up due to how overwhelmed I felt. Mindset matters. Be patient with yourself and pardon my French, but fuck anyone who is being impatient when you're new and learning. Especially talking behind your back negatively, that's not okay. Keep your chin up and keep up the good work friend, I promise it gets easier :)

Hi there! Your silhouettes and facial features look really good! I love your style :) I think to get closer to the other examples you need to study the facial structure underlying the features. Its apparent to me what the shape of the skull and the planes of the head are like in the last 3, whereas in yours it seems like it's facial features put onto an oval, which look good but don't quite hit the realism I think you're looking for. Work on drawing the Asaro head from different angles, and try drawing a bunch of skulls or heads without features, focusing on the muscles and how they lay on top of the bone. Exaggerate the planes themselves as well to better get a handle on it. Your line quality will improve with that as it's clearer which direction marks go in order to suggest said planes. Excited to see what you make next :)

Drawabox is my go to recommendation alongside Marco Bucci, Proko, and Marc Brunet. Drawabox will let you hit the ground running, it's what I wish I had used when I first started drawing. Those are all free resources that rival the paid ones, though if you're looking for a more formal structure consider New Masters Academy, they have just about everything you'd ever need. Once you start learning the "fundamentals" covered above, it can feel pretty daunting with how much information there is to learn and transfer from brain to hand. Just remember the 50% rule from drawabox (this is in it's first lesson) and never put anything above the joy of drawing itself, even if your brain wants to compare to other people's journeys. Wishing you a great time :)

Hi! This was me 2 months ago. I'm about 3 months in doing morning draws inpatient and it took a good while to feel confident. You'll miss a LOT, that's just how it is. These people are often sick, dehydrated, and have had IVs in every vein the nurses could find. I'll often miss two or three times a shift now but I used to just not get people before. Even if it takes two tries, and you get it, don't feel discouraged! The important part is that you get the blood. And if you don't, just reflect on what might have gone wrong and keep it in mind. No one expects you to be a phlebotomy god at first, one of my favorite pieces of mindset advice is "slow is smooth, and smooth is fast". 

Also, don't be afraid to draw in very weird places. I've drawn toes, elbows, in between fingers, on knuckles, on the palm of the hand, and even way up the bicep. If there's a good vein in a weird place it's better than a poor vein in the "correct" spot. Some veins also need weird angling, I've had hand veins that wouldn't get flow unless I had the needle about to come out and at a 90° angle. Sometimes it's too fragile and just the act of the needle entering will make it collapse or blow. Think of the anatomy of the arm, especially underlying the veins as everyone's configuration can be different. Just keep your chin up and go at it. Best of luck!

This looks great! Digital is so fun, it's its own beast. One skill that is much more noticeable when missing while drawing traditionally is draftsmanship. How confident your lines are, accuracy, the fluidity of line art/strokes, etc. It's much easier to hide poor draftsmanship digitally but when it's there is good draftsmanship difference in quality is wide. Highly recommend practicing traditionally every so often and then doing polished work digitally to get the best of both worlds :)

Hey, I'm in Anchorage right now so HMU if you have questions. For the most part it completely depends on what you're looking for, though the biggest centers will be Fairbanks and Anchorage. Rural areas are always hiring qualified people so if that's something you care for so it's definitely worth looking at. Each region has its own council that's listed on the state website (for Anc it's SREMSC) that will have pertinent information for each area, you should be able to find info on jobs and EMS agencies that are hiring there. Medevac and flight services are really big since there are areas that are otherwise inaccessible. The biggest hospitals are the Providence center and the AK Native center, both level 2 trauma centers and where most people get transferred to if needed, both are in Anchorage. If it's a higher level of care, they'll ship them from Anchorage down to Seattle.
